1	---
     2	key: lu2025lab
     3	status: ready
     4	evidence_basis: full-text
     5	design: empirical evaluation; within/cross-dataset DL training + temporally separated OOD test of DL and off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs
     6	dataset: Juliet, Devign, BigVul, ICVul (train/test); VentiVul (new; Linux+Chromium CVEs disclosed from 2025-05-01) for OOD
     7	sample_size: 4 DL models x 4 datasets; VentiVul 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 263 vulnerable-patched pairs; 4 LLMs x 3 prompts
     8	metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1; CVE Detection Rate (CDR); Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC); t-SNE centroid distance
     9	main_finding: DL F1 up to 91-94.5 in-distribution falls to 3.47-8.65 on temporally separated VentiVul; open-weight LLMs reach only 0.79-5.36 conservative F1; PACC <6% for all.
    10	relevance: high
    11	analysed: 2026-11-12
    12	---
    13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
    14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
    15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
    16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
    17	
    18	# From Lab to Reality: A Practical Evaluation of Deep Learning Models and LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
    19	
    20	- Authors: Lu, Chaomeng; Lagaisse, Bert
    21	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
    22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2512.10485 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10485
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
    30	- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.
    31	
    32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    33	- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
    34	- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
    35	- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
    36	- No formal hypotheses.
    37	
    38	## 3. Methodology
    39	- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
    40	- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
    41	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.
    42	
    43	## 4. Dataset and sample
    44	- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
    45	- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
    46	- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] With 263 vulnerable functions in 13,326, VentiVul prevalence is about 2.0%. We infer this from p. 4; the paper does not state the positive count for Whole-File.
    47	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
    48	- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).
    49	
    50	## 5. Experimental setup
    51	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
    52	- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).
    53	
    54	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    55	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
    56	- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs; LLMs use one deterministic run (p. 8) and DL results come from single training runs (seeds for DL not reported).
    57	
    58	## 7. Key findings
    59	1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). Accuracy is therefore misleading at 6% prevalence.
    60	2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
    61	3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
    62	4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
    63	5. DL vs LLM on the same OOD data [V/I] — best DL F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [I] Both families are close to an all-positive predictor at ~2% prevalence (F1 ≈ 3.9%, our calculation from p. 4 counts); LineVul (Devign) at recall 100%, precision 2%, F1 3.93 is effectively that predictor (p. 13, Table 7).
    64	6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
    65	7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
    66	8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
    67	9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).
    68	
    69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    70	- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
    71	- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
    72	- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
    73	- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).
    74	- [A] VentiVul is C/C++ only (Linux, Chromium) and may not generalise to other languages or proprietary code. "Unrelated" functions may hide other vulnerabilities (residual label noise), and regex function extraction can miss complex C/C++ syntax, which mainly affects Whole-File (p. 17).
    75	
    76	## 9. Limitations we identified
    77	- [I] No trivial baseline. At ~2% prevalence an all-positive classifier scores F1 ≈ 3.9%, so most reported DL and LLM F1 values (3.09–8.65) are at or barely above chance. The paper describes them as "low" but never compares them with chance.
    78	- [I] The DL and LLM comparison is asymmetric. DL models were trained on historical data; LLMs were used zero/few-shot without fine-tuning, with small open-weight models (MoE models with 2.4–3B active parameters) and Qwen3 thinking disabled (p. 5, p. 8). The study says nothing about frontier or fine-tuned LLMs, and nothing about LLMs in-distribution, because LLMs were not run on the four benchmarks.
    79	- [I] LLM precision/recall are not reported (Table 8 gives F1, CDR, PACC only, p. 14), so we cannot tell whether LLMs fail through false positives or false negatives.
    80	- [I] Single run, no confidence intervals; with 263 pairs, PACC differences of a few points (e.g. 5.34% vs 5.75%) are within noise.
    81	- [I] One function at a time with no context (p. 7). This is fair between families but disadvantages LLMs, which may need inter-procedural context. Many Linux/Chromium bugs need cross-function reasoning (cf. CVE-2025-37777 spanning two files, p. 4).
    82	- [I] No static-analysis tool is evaluated, although the introduction positions learning-based detection as a complement to static analysis (p. 1).
    83	- [I] Preprint status: arXiv v4 dated 4 Nov 2026 carries a footnote "accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software" (p. 1). Acceptance is author-stated; no journal DOI is in metadata.
    84	
    85	## 10. Threats to validity
    86	- Internal: [I] Deduplication within datasets and fixed test sets are reported (p. 7), but split ratios and cross-dataset overlap checks are not reported (Devign is from FFmpeg/QEMU and BigVul from open-source C/C++ repositories, p. 3, so project overlap is possible but unchecked). ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), which may inflate or deflate its numbers relative to LineVul.
    87	- External: [I] C/C++, two very large projects, 200 CVEs, open-weight mid-size LLMs only (p. 4, p. 5).
    88	- Construct: [I] Labelling unrelated same-file functions as non-vulnerable (p. 4) is a realistic construct for "scan the whole file", though label noise remains (p. 17). PACC is a strict and useful measure of patch sensitivity. CDR rewards indiscriminate positive prediction, as the paper itself shows (p. 13).
    89	- Statistical conclusion: [I] No tests, single runs, small per-CWE cells (p. 14).
    90	- Reproducibility: [I] Good: data, code and results are public (p. 2), and decoding settings and prompts are fully given (p. 8, p. 9). DL hyper-parameters are given only by reference to the original implementations (p. 8).
    91	
    92	## 11. Future research directions
    93	- Stated by authors [A]: representations and training that emphasise security-relevant changes, e.g. vulnerable–patched pair supervision (p. 16); datasets prioritising reliable labels, diverse patterns and explicit vulnerability–fix links over size (p. 16); complementing within-dataset evaluation with cross-dataset and temporally separated testing, and reporting CDR and patch-pair metrics with function-level metrics (p. 16); studying individual dataset factors, broader ecosystems and "more advanced LLM adaptation strategies" (p. 16).
    94	- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and frontier/fine-tuned LLMs on VentiVul with file/repository context and a chance baseline. That would give exactly the same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison our RQ5 identifies as missing.
    95	
    96	## 12. Relevance to our research
    97	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (DL vs LLM on same OOD data), RQ2 (temporal separation, cross-dataset shift, class ratio, accuracy vs F1), RQ4 (per-project and per-CWE variation, C/C++), RQ5 (patch-pair sensitivity, chance baselines).
    98	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the strongest direct evidence in our set that in-distribution DL scores (F1 91–94.5) do not survive temporal and dataset shift (F1 3.5–8.7). Off-the-shelf mid-size LLMs do no better than the shifted DL detectors, and both sit near chance. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking, and agrees with the PrimeVul near-random pair results (ding2025vulnerability). It covers no SAST tool or cost, so it adds nothing for RQ3.
    99	
   100	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   101	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |

                        real-world effectiveness remains underexplored. Recent work suggests that graph neural network-based and transformer-based
                        models, including large language models (LLMs), yield promising results when evaluated on curated benchmark datasets. These

                        benchmarks and real-world deployment, emphasizing the value of our deployment-oriented evaluation framework and the need for

input.message:
Critical review: qin2026review and lu2025lab (project 2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis)

I did not write the report file because the harness blocks subagent writes. The intended path was /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/research/2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis/reports/critical-review-2026-11-12-C.md, since -A and -B already exist.

**Result: 0 pass, 2 fix needed** (qin2026review, lu2025lab). Neither is ready to move to `complete`.

**Checks run**
- `rlab validate`: both papers are verified and the PDF identity matches (DOI printed in qin's PDF; arXiv id printed in lu's PDF). Neither is retracted.
- `rlab cite-check` on both analysis.md files: OK.
- Every number in each Key findings section was grepped against fulltext.txt.
- Qin's Figures 1–2 were rendered from the PDF, because pdftotext drops them. They match the analysis.
- Qin's OpenAlex venue facts were re-queried and match: no host organisation, not in DOAJ, not core, published 2026-10-29.
- Qin's PrimeVul ranges were checked against ding2025vulnerability Table V (p. 7). All six ranges match: 62.88–68.26, 1.91–5.82, 18.05–21.43, VD-S 88.78–91.51, P-C 1.06–3.01, P-B 84.22–88.30.

---

## qin2026review — FIX NEEDED

Most numbers and quotes are correct, and the venue appraisal is good. The problems are labels, one miscount, a claim of "independent" corroboration, and the analysis not noticing that qin misrepresents a source we hold.

1. **§5, line 49: wrong label and wrong word.**
   - Problem: "[V] One quantitative re-analysis: the review re-reads PrimeVul Table V…". These are the review re-reporting another paper's numbers. That is [A] under the standards, not [V]. It is also not a re-analysis. The [I] note undersells our check: it says only "the 68.26%/3.09% pair matches", but all ranges match.
   - Evidence: qin p. 12; ding2025vulnerability fulltext p. 7, Table V.
   - Fix: "[A] The review re-reports PrimeVul Table V for five code LMs: … (p. 12). [I] All six ranges (F1 three settings, VD-S, P-C, P-B) match ding2025vulnerability Table V (p. 7). Cite ding directly for these numbers."

2. **§13, row 2: strength.**
   - Problem: the row is rated "moderate" for a secondary re-report.
   - Fix: change the strength to "weak (secondary; cite [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7] for the evidence itself)". Otherwise the same PrimeVul numbers get counted twice.

3. **§4, line 44: miscount.**
   - Problem: "Table 1 lists 11 representative methods". Table 1 lists 12: Devign, CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, LineVul, GRACE, EnStack, DLAP, Finetuning LLM, LLMVulExp, Cross-project zero-shot, Context-Enhanced, M2CVD. Four of those are not LLM-based (Devign, CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, LineVul). "Roughly a dozen are LLM-based detection studies" also undercounts the references.
   - Evidence: pp. 6–7 (Table 1); reference list pp. 14–16.
   - Fix: "Table 1 lists 12 methods, 8 of them LLM-based (pp. 6–7). About 16 of the 32 references are LLM-based detection or evaluation studies ([6], [10]–[13], [15], [23]–[32]; [16] unclear)."

4. **§7 finding 5, line 61: wrong page, and a misrepresentation the analysis misses.**
   - Wrong page: "[1] … [15] (p. 15)". Reference [1] is on p. 14.
   - Thin support: [1] (Li et al., TDSC 2024) evaluates SAST tools only. So qin's plural "unified benchmarks" rests on a single LLM-vs-SAST study, [15].
   - Misrepresentation: [15] is gnieciak2025large, which is in our project. Its headline result is LLM mean F1 0.75–0.80 vs SAST 0.26–0.55, and it recommends a hybrid (gnieciak analysis §7.1; gnieciak fulltext p. 1). Qin's summary leaves out that LLMs scored higher than SAST, and "SAST is usually more stable" is not a finding of [15].
   - Fix: change the page to "(p. 14, p. 15)". Add: "[I] [1] is a SAST-only study; the only LLM-vs-SAST source is [15] = gnieciak2025large, which reports LLMs above SAST on F1 (0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55) [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. Qin's summary leaves out that LLMs scored higher. Use gnieciak directly; do not cite qin for this comparison."

5. **§12, line 92: "corroborate our RQ2 answer independently" is wrong.**
   - Problem: qin cites three papers that are in our project: [14] = ding2025vulnerability, [15] = gnieciak2025large, [21] = sheng2025llms. Its inflation argument relies on ding (pp. 2, 10, 12).
   - Fix: "Its recommendations agree with our RQ2 answer, but they are not independent. It relies largely on ding2025vulnerability [14], which we cite directly, and it also cites gnieciak2025large [15] and sheng2025llms [21]. Do not count it as an extra source."

6. **§7 finding 4, line 60: label.**
   - Problem: "[V, table content]" is attached to Table 2. Table 2 is the author's own normative risk matrix (mechanisms, signals, mitigations), not data.
   - Fix: change the label to "[A] (pp. 10–11)".

7. **§2 line 35 and §9 line 77: overstated wording.**
   - Problem: the analysis calls three questions vs four RQs "internally inconsistent". The p. 2 framing questions and the p. 4 formal RQs work at different levels, and p. 4 maps the four RQs onto its own framing. The undefined "C2" (p. 12) is a real defect; grep finds no C1, C2 or C3 anywhere else.
   - Fix: "The introduction frames three guiding questions (p. 2) and Section 3.1 sets four formal RQs (p. 4). The two are not explicitly reconciled. 'Medium confidence to C2' (p. 12) refers to a claim label that is never defined."

8. **Header, line 21: venue status not flagged.**
   - Problem: "2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (published)" has no caveat, and this line feeds readers before they reach the Analyst notes.
   - Fix: "2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (Zeus Press; published, peer review not documented, low-visibility venue — see Analyst notes)".

9. **§9 and §10: the threats section misses the source-dependence problem.**
   - Problem: the corpus-selection threat is generic. The specific one is that qin's two quantitative pillars (PrimeVul and LLM-vs-SAST) are each one study, and both are in our corpus.
   - Fix: add to §10 Internal: "[I] Quantitative claims rest on single studies we already hold (ding2025vulnerability for inflation, gnieciak2025large for LLM vs SAST), so the review adds framing but no evidence."

---

## lu2025lab — FIX NEEDED

Numbers are accurate: all Table 5–8 values cited were checked. The main problems:
- a published JSS version exists and the analysis says none was found;
- the chance-baseline paragraph quotes the wrong F1 range and misses that most LLM configurations score below chance;
- "same data" claims ignore ReVeal's subset;
- evidence strengths are too high for a preprint.

1. **Venue status (line 21; §9 last bullet, line 83; Analyst notes, line 122): a published version exists.**
   - Evidence: Crossref has "From lab to reality: A practical evaluation of deep learning models and LLMs for vulnerability detection", Lu & Lagaisse, Journal of Systems and Software, article 113185, Nov 2026, DOI 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185. Queried 2026-11-12. OpenAlex W4417296041 still lists only arXiv and Figshare. There is also an SSRN copy, 10.2139/ssrn.6066377.
   - Standards §3 say to use the published version when one exists.
   - Fix:
     - Run `rlab add 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185` and let rlab verify it. Check OA; if it is not OA, keep the arXiv v4 text as the page source.
     - Update line 21 to "2025 arXiv preprint; published in J. Systems and Software 2026 (doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185); page refs = arXiv v4".
     - Replace the §9 bullet and the Analyst note with a peer-reviewed status (once verified) and a note that v4 is the accepted manuscript (footnote, p. 1). Log it.

2. **§9 bullet 1 (line 77): chance-baseline paragraph has the wrong range and misses below-chance results.**
   - Problem: "most reported DL and LLM F1 values (3.09–8.65) are at or barely above chance". The LLM conservative F1 range is 0.79–5.36, not 3.09+. 7 of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values are below the all-positive F1: 3.72, 2.95, 3.04, 4.29 (above), 3.64, 4.89 (above), 3.09, 0.79, 1.39, 4.07 (above), 5.36 (above), 4.71 (above). So most LLM configurations score below a predictor that flags everything.
   - Evidence: Table 8, p. 14.
   - Your arithmetic is correct: 2p/(1+p) with p = 263/13,326 = 1.974% gives 3.87%.
   - Fix: "[I] At p = 263/13,326 = 1.97% (p. 4) an all-positive classifier has F1 = 2p/(1+p) = 3.87%. All 8 DL F1 values (3.47–8.65, Table 7 p. 13) are at most 4.8 points above it. 7 of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values (Table 8, p. 14) are below it. The paper never compares results with chance."

3. **Baseline vs the paper's actual prevalence: ReVeal's subset is different.**
   - Table 7's Accuracy, Precision and Recall together pin down the prevalence each model was scored on.
   - All four LineVul rows give 1.97%, which equals 263/13,326. This confirms the Whole-File positive count. You can drop the line 124 "we assume 263" uncertainty and the line 46 "the paper does not state the positive count" caveat. Restate them as "consistent with Table 7 A/P/R".
   - All four ReVeal rows give 1.79%. ReVeal is scored on its processable subset (p. 7), so its all-positive F1 is about 3.52%, not 3.9%. RV(ICVul) at F1 3.47 is below its own chance level; RV(Devign) 3.86 and RV(Juliet) 3.97 are about 0.35–0.45 above it.
   - Fix: add to §4, line 46: "[I] Back-calculated from Table 7 (p. 13): LineVul rows imply prevalence 1.97% (= 263/13,326); ReVeal rows imply 1.79% on its processable subset, so its all-positive F1 ≈ 3.5%."

4. **Chance level for PACC and CDR is missing.**
   - All-positive gives CDR 100% and PACC 0%. A random classifier flagging a fraction q of functions has expected PACC q(1−q), which is 25% at q = 0.5. Every model's PACC (≤5.75%) is far below a coin flip. That means the models give the same label to the vulnerable and patched versions; it is not "near chance".
   - §7.5 (line 63), §12 (line 98: "both sit near chance") and §13 row 5 should name the metric.
   - Fix:
     - "Near the all-positive F1 baseline; on PACC all models are far below a random-guess baseline (q(1−q), up to 25%), i.e. they label vulnerable and patched versions alike [I]."
     - Change "chance baselines" under RQ5 (line 97) accordingly.

5. **"Same data" claims (§7.5 heading, line 63; §13 row 4, line 106: "On the same VentiVul functions").**
   - Problem: ReVeal metrics cover only the functions it can process (p. 7). Its implied prevalence differs (1.79% vs 1.97%), and the subset size is not reported. Few-shot test sets exclude the demonstration pairs (p. 8). Valid-only LLM results cover only parseable outputs (p. 8).
   - Fix: replace with "on VentiVul (ReVeal scored on its processable subset, size not reported, p. 7; few-shot excludes demonstration pairs, p. 8)".
   - Also add to §7.5: best DL vs best LLM is ReVeal-BigVul 8.65 (≈2.5× its 3.5% chance level) vs Mistral few-shot 5.36 (≈1.4× 3.87%). This is [I].

6. **§13 strengths (lines 103–111): too high, and one claim goes beyond the study.**
   - Problem: rows are rated "moderate" on a preprint with single runs, no CIs and no tests. Standards §5 say "preprint without replication" = weak.
   - Fix: rate the rows weak, or moderate only after finding 1 confirms JSS publication. If moderate, justify it explicitly, e.g. "the cross-dataset drop agrees with ding2025vulnerability and chakraborty2024revisiting".
   - Row 5 also says "no family is practically usable on recent CVEs". That generalises beyond the study, which tested 2 DL families and 4 open-weight LLMs of at most 32B, function-only input, no SAST, no frontier models. Rescope to "neither the evaluated DL detectors nor the four off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs".

7. **§7 finding 1 (line 59): unlabelled inference.**
   - Problem: "Accuracy is therefore misleading at 6% prevalence" sits unlabelled inside a [V] item.
   - Fix: "[A] Predictions biased toward the majority class give high accuracy with few detections (p. 11)."

8. **§3, line 41: few-shot k overstated.**
   - Problem: "few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs)". The paper says "With k = 4, for example, the prompt contains four demonstration functions…" (p. 8). The k actually used is not stated unambiguously.
   - Fix: "few-shot with a fixed, project- and class-balanced set of demonstrations from complete pairs; k = 4 is given 'for example' (p. 8), actual k not explicitly stated".

9. **§5, line 56, and §9, line 80: unsupported "single run" claim for DL.**
   - Problem: "DL results come from single training runs" is not stated in the paper; grep finds no runs, seeds or epochs for DL. LLMs are single deterministic runs (p. 8).
   - Fix: "Number of DL training runs and seeds: not reported. LLMs: one deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8)."

10. **Conflict of interest and funding not appraised (§10 / Analyst notes).**
    - Problem: ICVul, one of the four training datasets, is the authors' own (Lu, C., Li, T., Dehaene, T., Lagaisse, B., MSR 2025; reference list pp. 18–19), and the paper calls it "a high-quality software vulnerability dataset" (p. 3). No funding or acknowledgement section exists (grep). Standards §5 require a COI check.
    - Fix: add "[I] ICVul is the authors' own dataset (p. 3; refs pp. 18–19); funding: not reported."

11. **§10 Internal (line 86): a VentiVul-specific overlap threat is missing.**
    - Problem: temporal separation applies to the CVE fixes. About 98% of Whole-File functions are unchanged same-file functions (13,063 of 13,326). Older versions of these may appear in BigVul/ICVul training data, which are mined from open-source C/C++ fix commits (p. 3), and in LLM pretraining. The paper does not report checking whether Linux or Chromium code is in the training benchmarks.
    - Fix: "[I] Overlap between VentiVul's unchanged functions and the Linux/Chromium code that BigVul or ICVul may contain is not checked (p. 3, p. 4). This could change Whole-File false-positive rates and adds to LLM contamination risk."

12. **§9 bullet 5 (line 81): "many" is unsupported.**
    - Problem: "Many Linux/Chromium bugs need cross-function reasoning" rests on one example.
    - Fix: "Some CVEs span several functions/files (263 pairs over 200 CVEs, so up to 63 CVEs are multi-function; e.g. CVE-2025-37777, p. 4). How many need cross-function reasoning is not reported."

13. **§10 Reproducibility (line 90): "prompts are fully given" is overstated.**
    - Problem: Table 4 gives prompt templates. The system prompt is only paraphrased (p. 8), and the demonstration functions are not listed in the paper.
    - Fix: "Prompt templates given (Table 4, p. 9); system prompt paraphrased and demonstrations not listed in the paper (repository not checked)."

14. **Frontmatter main_finding (line 9) and §12 (line 98): conflation and overclaim.**
    - Problem: "DL F1 up to 91–94.5 in-distribution falls to 3.47–8.65". The 94.14 is VulBERTa, which was never run on VentiVul. §12 calls the paper "the strongest direct evidence in our set", which is too strong for a single-run study pending peer-review confirmation, when ding2025vulnerability shows the same drop.
    - Fix:
      - main_finding: "LineVul F1 91–94.5 in-distribution falls to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul (all 8 ReVeal/LineVul configs 3.47–8.65)…"
      - §12: "direct evidence, consistent with ding2025vulnerability".

15. **§7 finding 8 and §13 row 7: missing qualifier on LLM per-project results.**
    - Problem: the LLM per-project CDR/PACC figures are zero-shot, valid-only (p. 13), and the analysis doesn't say so.
    - Fix: add "(LLMs: zero-shot, valid-only, p. 13)".

16. **§8 (lines 70–74): minor omissions from the authors' stated limitations.**
    - Fix: add "VentiVul does not contain every vulnerability in the selected versions; model coverage limited by reproducibility and compute; Function-Pair less exposed to label noise than Whole-File (p. 17)".

The known `added_reason` metadata error was not re-reported.

---

## Cross-paper observations

1. **Contradiction to record in the evidence matrix.** CodeBERT fine-tuned on BigVul, tested in-distribution:
   - lu2025lab: LineVul (CodeBERT) F1 91.00 (p. 12, Table 6).
   - ding2025vulnerability: CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 (p. 7, Table V).
   - Same model family and benchmark, 28 points apart. Neither paper explains it. A likely [I] explanation is different splits and preprocessing (lu used LineVul's original pipeline, p. 8).

2. **Consistent pattern.** BigVul-trained models collapse on newer or cleaner data:
   - ding BV→PrimeVul F1 1.91–5.82 (p. 7);
   - lu LineVul(BigVul)→VentiVul F1 6.87 (p. 13).
   - Both should be read against the chance level. If ding's numbers are used next to lu's, compute PrimeVul's all-positive F1 the same way.

3. **Double-counting risk.**
   - qin2026review cites ding2025vulnerability [14], gnieciak2025large [15] and sheng2025llms [21].
   - lu2025lab builds its motivation on ding and chakraborty2024revisiting.
   - Qin should not be counted as independent support for RQ1 or RQ2.

4. **Qin vs gnieciak.** Qin's "SAST more stable; complementarity" summary of the LLM-vs-SAST evidence leaves out that its only head-to-head source (gnieciak2025large) reports LLMs scoring higher on F1. If qin is cited for positioning, record this in the evidence matrix Contradictions section.

## qin2026review — FIX NEEDED

Most numbers and quotes are correct, and the venue appraisal is good. The problems are labels, one miscount, a claim of "independent" corroboration, and the analysis not noticing that qin misrepresents a source we hold.

1. **§5, line 49: wrong label and wrong word.**
   - Problem: "[V] One quantitative re-analysis: the review re-reads PrimeVul Table V…". These are the review re-reporting another paper's numbers. That is [A] under the standards, not [V]. It is also not a re-analysis. The [I] note undersells our check: it says only "the 68.26%/3.09% pair matches", but all ranges match.
   - Evidence: qin p. 12; ding2025vulnerability fulltext p. 7, Table V.
   - Fix: "[A] The review re-reports PrimeVul Table V for five code LMs: … (p. 12). [I] All six ranges (F1 three settings, VD-S, P-C, P-B) match ding2025vulnerability Table V (p. 7). Cite ding directly for these numbers."

2. **§13, row 2: strength.**
   - Problem: the row is rated "moderate" for a secondary re-report.
   - Fix: change the strength to "weak (secondary; cite [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7] for the evidence itself)". Otherwise the same PrimeVul numbers get counted twice.

3. **§4, line 44: miscount.**
   - Problem: "Table 1 lists 11 representative methods". Table 1 lists 12: Devign, CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, LineVul, GRACE, EnStack, DLAP, Finetuning LLM, LLMVulExp, Cross-project zero-shot, Context-Enhanced, M2CVD. Four of those are not LLM-based (Devign, CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, LineVul). "Roughly a dozen are LLM-based detection studies" also undercounts the references.
   - Evidence: pp. 6–7 (Table 1); reference list pp. 14–16.
   - Fix: "Table 1 lists 12 methods, 8 of them LLM-based (pp. 6–7). About 16 of the 32 references are LLM-based detection or evaluation studies ([6], [10]–[13], [15], [23]–[32]; [16] unclear)."

4. **§7 finding 5, line 61: wrong page, and a misrepresentation the analysis misses.**
   - Wrong page: "[1] … [15] (p. 15)". Reference [1] is on p. 14.
   - Thin support: [1] (Li et al., TDSC 2024) evaluates SAST tools only. So qin's plural "unified benchmarks" rests on a single LLM-vs-SAST study, [15].
   - Misrepresentation: [15] is gnieciak2025large, which is in our project. Its headline result is LLM mean F1 0.75–0.80 vs SAST 0.26–0.55, and it recommends a hybrid (gnieciak analysis §7.1; gnieciak fulltext p. 1). Qin's summary leaves out that LLMs scored higher than SAST, and "SAST is usually more stable" is not a finding of [15].
   - Fix: change the page to "(p. 14, p. 15)". Add: "[I] [1] is a SAST-only study; the only LLM-vs-SAST source is [15] = gnieciak2025large, which reports LLMs above SAST on F1 (0.75–0.80 vs 0.26–0.55) [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10]. Qin's summary leaves out that LLMs scored higher. Use gnieciak directly; do not cite qin for this comparison."

5. **§12, line 92: "corroborate our RQ2 answer independently" is wrong.**
   - Problem: qin cites three papers that are in our project: [14] = ding2025vulnerability, [15] = gnieciak2025large, [21] = sheng2025llms. Its inflation argument relies on ding (pp. 2, 10, 12).
   - Fix: "Its recommendations agree with our RQ2 answer, but they are not independent. It relies largely on ding2025vulnerability [14], which we cite directly, and it also cites gnieciak2025large [15] and sheng2025llms [21]. Do not count it as an extra source."

6. **§7 finding 4, line 60: label.**
   - Problem: "[V, table content]" is attached to Table 2. Table 2 is the author's own normative risk matrix (mechanisms, signals, mitigations), not data.
   - Fix: change the label to "[A] (pp. 10–11)".

7. **§2 line 35 and §9 line 77: overstated wording.**
   - Problem: the analysis calls three questions vs four RQs "internally inconsistent". The p. 2 framing questions and the p. 4 formal RQs work at different levels, and p. 4 maps the four RQs onto its own framing. The undefined "C2" (p. 12) is a real defect; grep finds no C1, C2 or C3 anywhere else.
   - Fix: "The introduction frames three guiding questions (p. 2) and Section 3.1 sets four formal RQs (p. 4). The two are not explicitly reconciled. 'Medium confidence to C2' (p. 12) refers to a claim label that is never defined."

8. **Header, line 21: venue status not flagged.**
   - Problem: "2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (published)" has no caveat, and this line feeds readers before they reach the Analyst notes.
   - Fix: "2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (Zeus Press; published, peer review not documented, low-visibility venue — see Analyst notes)".

9. **§9 and §10: the threats section misses the source-dependence problem.**
   - Problem: the corpus-selection threat is generic. The specific one is that qin's two quantitative pillars (PrimeVul and LLM-vs-SAST) are each one study, and both are in our corpus.
   - Fix: add to §10 Internal: "[I] Quantitative claims rest on single studies we already hold (ding2025vulnerability for inflation, gnieciak2025large for LLM vs SAST), so the review adds framing but no evidence."

## lu2025lab — FIX NEEDED

Numbers are accurate: all Table 5–8 values cited were checked. The main problems:
- a published JSS version exists and the analysis says none was found;
- the chance-baseline paragraph quotes the wrong F1 range and misses that most LLM configurations score below chance;
- "same data" claims ignore ReVeal's subset;
- evidence strengths are too high for a preprint.

1. **Venue status (line 21; §9 last bullet, line 83; Analyst notes, line 122): a published version exists.**
   - Evidence: Crossref has "From lab to reality: A practical evaluation of deep learning models and LLMs for vulnerability detection", Lu & Lagaisse, Journal of Systems and Software, article 113185, Nov 2026, DOI 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185. Queried 2026-11-12. OpenAlex W4417296041 still lists only arXiv and Figshare. There is also an SSRN copy, 10.2139/ssrn.6066377.
   - Standards §3 say to use the published version when one exists.
   - Fix:
     - Run `rlab add 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185` and let rlab verify it. Check OA; if it is not OA, keep the arXiv v4 text as the page source.
     - Update line 21 to "2025 arXiv preprint; published in J. Systems and Software 2026 (doi 10.1016/j.jss.2026.113185); page refs = arXiv v4".
     - Replace the §9 bullet and the Analyst note with a peer-reviewed status (once verified) and a note that v4 is the accepted manuscript (footnote, p. 1). Log it.

2. **§9 bullet 1 (line 77): chance-baseline paragraph has the wrong range and misses below-chance results.**
   - Problem: "most reported DL and LLM F1 values (3.09–8.65) are at or barely above chance". The LLM conservative F1 range is 0.79–5.36, not 3.09+. 7 of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values are below the all-positive F1: 3.72, 2.95, 3.04, 4.29 (above), 3.64, 4.89 (above), 3.09, 0.79, 1.39, 4.07 (above), 5.36 (above), 4.71 (above). So most LLM configurations score below a predictor that flags everything.
   - Evidence: Table 8, p. 14.
   - Your arithmetic is correct: 2p/(1+p) with p = 263/13,326 = 1.974% gives 3.87%.
   - Fix: "[I] At p = 263/13,326 = 1.97% (p. 4) an all-positive classifier has F1 = 2p/(1+p) = 3.87%. All 8 DL F1 values (3.47–8.65, Table 7 p. 13) are at most 4.8 points above it. 7 of the 12 LLM conservative F1 values (Table 8, p. 14) are below it. The paper never compares results with chance."

3. **Baseline vs the paper's actual prevalence: ReVeal's subset is different.**
   - Table 7's Accuracy, Precision and Recall together pin down the prevalence each model was scored on.
   - All four LineVul rows give 1.97%, which equals 263/13,326. This confirms the Whole-File positive count. You can drop the line 124 "we assume 263" uncertainty and the line 46 "the paper does not state the positive count" caveat. Restate them as "consistent with Table 7 A/P/R".
   - All four ReVeal rows give 1.79%. ReVeal is scored on its processable subset (p. 7), so its all-positive F1 is about 3.52%, not 3.9%. RV(ICVul) at F1 3.47 is below its own chance level; RV(Devign) 3.86 and RV(Juliet) 3.97 are about 0.35–0.45 above it.
   - Fix: add to §4, line 46: "[I] Back-calculated from Table 7 (p. 13): LineVul rows imply prevalence 1.97% (= 263/13,326); ReVeal rows imply 1.79% on its processable subset, so its all-positive F1 ≈ 3.5%."

4. **Chance level for PACC and CDR is missing.**
   - All-positive gives CDR 100% and PACC 0%. A random classifier flagging a fraction q of functions has expected PACC q(1−q), which is 25% at q = 0.5. Every model's PACC (≤5.75%) is far below a coin flip. That means the models give the same label to the vulnerable and patched versions; it is not "near chance".
   - §7.5 (line 63), §12 (line 98: "both sit near chance") and §13 row 5 should name the metric.
   - Fix:
     - "Near the all-positive F1 baseline; on PACC all models are far below a random-guess baseline (q(1−q), up to 25%), i.e. they label vulnerable and patched versions alike [I]."
     - Change "chance baselines" under RQ5 (line 97) accordingly.

5. **"Same data" claims (§7.5 heading, line 63; §13 row 4, line 106: "On the same VentiVul functions").**
   - Problem: ReVeal metrics cover only the functions it can process (p. 7). Its implied prevalence differs (1.79% vs 1.97%), and the subset size is not reported. Few-shot test sets exclude the demonstration pairs (p. 8). Valid-only LLM results cover only parseable outputs (p. 8).
   - Fix: replace with "on VentiVul (ReVeal scored on its processable subset, size not reported, p. 7; few-shot excludes demonstration pairs, p. 8)".
   - Also add to §7.5: best DL vs best LLM is ReVeal-BigVul 8.65 (≈2.5× its 3.5% chance level) vs Mistral few-shot 5.36 (≈1.4× 3.87%). This is [I].

6. **§13 strengths (lines 103–111): too high, and one claim goes beyond the study.**
   - Problem: rows are rated "moderate" on a preprint with single runs, no CIs and no tests. Standards §5 say "preprint without replication" = weak.
   - Fix: rate the rows weak, or moderate only after finding 1 confirms JSS publication. If moderate, justify it explicitly, e.g. "the cross-dataset drop agrees with ding2025vulnerability and chakraborty2024revisiting".
   - Row 5 also says "no family is practically usable on recent CVEs". That generalises beyond the study, which tested 2 DL families and 4 open-weight LLMs of at most 32B, function-only input, no SAST, no frontier models. Rescope to "neither the evaluated DL detectors nor the four off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs".

7. **§7 finding 1 (line 59): unlabelled inference.**
   - Problem: "Accuracy is therefore misleading at 6% prevalence" sits unlabelled inside a [V] item.
   - Fix: "[A] Predictions biased toward the majority class give high accuracy with few detections (p. 11)."

8. **§3, line 41: few-shot k overstated.**
   - Problem: "few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs)". The paper says "With k = 4, for example, the prompt contains four demonstration functions…" (p. 8). The k actually used is not stated unambiguously.
   - Fix: "few-shot with a fixed, project- and class-balanced set of demonstrations from complete pairs; k = 4 is given 'for example' (p. 8), actual k not explicitly stated".

9. **§5, line 56, and §9, line 80: unsupported "single run" claim for DL.**
   - Problem: "DL results come from single training runs" is not stated in the paper; grep finds no runs, seeds or epochs for DL. LLMs are single deterministic runs (p. 8).
   - Fix: "Number of DL training runs and seeds: not reported. LLMs: one deterministic run (temperature 0, seed 42, p. 8)."

10. **Conflict of interest and funding not appraised (§10 / Analyst notes).**
    - Problem: ICVul, one of the four training datasets, is the authors' own (Lu, C., Li, T., Dehaene, T., Lagaisse, B., MSR 2025; reference list pp. 18–19), and the paper calls it "a high-quality software vulnerability dataset" (p. 3). No funding or acknowledgement section exists (grep). Standards §5 require a COI check.
    - Fix: add "[I] ICVul is the authors' own dataset (p. 3; refs pp. 18–19); funding: not reported."

11. **§10 Internal (line 86): a VentiVul-specific overlap threat is missing.**
    - Problem: temporal separation applies to the CVE fixes. About 98% of Whole-File functions are unchanged same-file functions (13,063 of 13,326). Older versions of these may appear in BigVul/ICVul training data, which are mined from open-source C/C++ fix commits (p. 3), and in LLM pretraining. The paper does not report checking whether Linux or Chromium code is in the training benchmarks.
    - Fix: "[I] Overlap between VentiVul's unchanged functions and the Linux/Chromium code that BigVul or ICVul may contain is not checked (p. 3, p. 4). This could change Whole-File false-positive rates and adds to LLM contamination risk."

12. **§9 bullet 5 (line 81): "many" is unsupported.**
    - Problem: "Many Linux/Chromium bugs need cross-function reasoning" rests on one example.
    - Fix: "Some CVEs span several functions/files (263 pairs over 200 CVEs, so up to 63 CVEs are multi-function; e.g. CVE-2025-37777, p. 4). How many need cross-function reasoning is not reported."

13. **§10 Reproducibility (line 90): "prompts are fully given" is overstated.**
    - Problem: Table 4 gives prompt templates. The system prompt is only paraphrased (p. 8), and the demonstration functions are not listed in the paper.
    - Fix: "Prompt templates given (Table 4, p. 9); system prompt paraphrased and demonstrations not listed in the paper (repository not checked)."

14. **Frontmatter main_finding (line 9) and §12 (line 98): conflation and overclaim.**
    - Problem: "DL F1 up to 91–94.5 in-distribution falls to 3.47–8.65". The 94.14 is VulBERTa, which was never run on VentiVul. §12 calls the paper "the strongest direct evidence in our set", which is too strong for a single-run study pending peer-review confirmation, when ding2025vulnerability shows the same drop.
    - Fix:
      - main_finding: "LineVul F1 91–94.5 in-distribution falls to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul (all 8 ReVeal/LineVul configs 3.47–8.65)…"
      - §12: "direct evidence, consistent with ding2025vulnerability".

15. **§7 finding 8 and §13 row 7: missing qualifier on LLM per-project results.**
    - Problem: the LLM per-project CDR/PACC figures are zero-shot, valid-only (p. 13), and the analysis doesn't say so.
    - Fix: add "(LLMs: zero-shot, valid-only, p. 13)".

16. **§8 (lines 70–74): minor omissions from the authors' stated limitations.**
    - Fix: add "VentiVul does not contain every vulnerability in the selected versions; model coverage limited by reproducibility and compute; Function-Pair less exposed to label noise than Whole-File (p. 17)".

The known `added_reason` metadata error was not re-reported.

## Cross-paper observations

1. **Contradiction to record in the evidence matrix.** CodeBERT fine-tuned on BigVul, tested in-distribution:
   - lu2025lab: LineVul (CodeBERT) F1 91.00 (p. 12, Table 6).
   - ding2025vulnerability: CodeBERT BV→BV F1 62.88 (p. 7, Table V).
   - Same model family and benchmark, 28 points apart. Neither paper explains it. A likely [I] explanation is different splits and preprocessing (lu used LineVul's original pipeline, p. 8).

2. **Consistent pattern.** BigVul-trained models collapse on newer or cleaner data:
   - ding BV→PrimeVul F1 1.91–5.82 (p. 7);
   - lu LineVul(BigVul)→VentiVul F1 6.87 (p. 13).
   - Both should be read against the chance level. If ding's numbers are used next to lu's, compute PrimeVul's all-positive F1 the same way.

3. **Double-counting risk.**
   - qin2026review cites ding2025vulnerability [14], gnieciak2025large [15] and sheng2025llms [21].
   - lu2025lab builds its motivation on ding and chakraborty2024revisiting.
   - Qin should not be counted as independent support for RQ1 or RQ2.

4. **Qin vs gnieciak.** Qin's "SAST more stable; complementarity" summary of the LLM-vs-SAST evidence leaves out that its only head-to-head source (gnieciak2025large) reports LLMs scoring higher on F1. If qin is cited for positioning, record this in the evidence matrix Contradictions section.
